timeline.note: Dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology anchored to 1 Kings 6:1 and the 40-year reigns credited to David and Solomon. Other evangelical chronological frameworks shift these dates by a decade or more.

Birth year is estimated from his description as a 'young man' at Stephen's stoning (c. AD 34) and as 'the aged' in Philemon (c. AD 60). The death date rests on early church tradition placing his execution in Rome under Nero, not on Scripture itself.

Birth year is estimated from his adult activity during Jesus' ministry (c. AD 27-30). The death date rests on early church tradition (Eusebius, Origen) placing his martyrdom in Rome under Nero, not on Scripture itself.

No birth or death year is given for Eleazar; his ministry spans from the wilderness wandering into the early settlement of Canaan, roughly the 15th-13th centuries BC depending on the framework used for the Exodus date.
No birth or death year is given for Phinehas; his defining act at Baal-peor falls in the wilderness period, with later appearances extending into the early settlement of Canaan.

timeline.note: 1 Samuel 13:1 states Saul's age at accession and length of reign, but the Hebrew numbers are textually corrupt (widely noted as a gap/scribal error in the manuscripts); Acts 13:21's round figure of "forty years" is the traditional total, commonly placed around 1050-1010 BC, but neither number rests on the same firm footing as the explicit accession-age formula used for Judah's later kings, so no specific date is plotted here.
Goliath's death occurs early in Saul's reign, before David's own reign began, roughly the 11th century BC by the traditional United Monarchy chronology.
No birth or death year is given for Gad; his appearances span from David's fugitive years to his old age, roughly the mid-1000s to mid-900s BC.
No birth or death year is given for Abiathar; his life spans Saul's reign through the early years of Solomon's, roughly the mid-1000s to mid-900s BC.

Mephibosheth is crippled as a child around the time of Saul and Jonathan's deaths and lives through the bulk of David's reign, roughly the 11th-10th centuries BC by the traditional United Monarchy chronology.
No birth or death year is given for Nathan; his ministry spans David's reign, roughly the late 1000s to mid-900s BC.
No birth or death year is given for Zadok; his ministry spans David's and Solomon's reigns, roughly the mid-1000s to mid-900s BC.

name: Barzillai
topics: loyalty in a king's darkest hour

timeline.note: The biblical regnal formula for Israel's kings (unlike Judah's) does not record an accession age, only reign length and synchronism to Judah's king — enough to fix roughly when Jeroboam reigned (c. 931-910 BC), but not his own birth or death year, so no specific date is plotted here.

1 Kings 14:21 states Rehoboam was 41 when he began to reign and reigned 17 years in Jerusalem; dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology, with other evangelical frameworks shifting these figures by a few years.
2 Kings 22:1 states Josiah was 8 when he began to reign and reigned 31 years in Jerusalem; dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology.

1 Kings 22:42 states Jehoshaphat was 35 when he began to reign and reigned 25 years in Jerusalem; dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology, with other evangelical frameworks shifting these figures by a few years.

Israel's regnal formula (unlike Judah's) gives reign length and synchronism to Judah's king but no accession age, so Ahab's own birth year is not calculable; his reign is conventionally placed c. 874-853 BC.
No birth or death year is given — Elijah did not die but was taken up in a whirlwind — so no specific date is plotted; his ministry falls under Ahab through Ahaziah, roughly the mid-800s BC.
Israel's regnal formula gives reign length and synchronism to Judah's king but no accession age, so Jehu's own birth year is not calculable; his 28-year reign is conventionally placed c. 841-814 BC.
No birth or death year is given for Elisha; his ministry spans several Israelite kings' reigns, roughly the mid-800s to early 700s BC.

2 Chronicles 24:15 states Jehoiada died at 130, an unusually long life, but without a fixed calendar anchor for his birth or death, so no specific date is plotted; his ministry falls under Athaliah's usurpation and Joash's early reign, roughly the mid-800s BC.

2 Kings 15:2 and 2 Chronicles 26:3 state Uzziah began to reign at 16 and reigned 52 years in Jerusalem; dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology, though evangelical chronologies vary somewhat on the exact overlap of his reign with his son Jotham's co-regency during his years of leprous isolation.
2 Kings 14:25 places Jonah's earlier ministry under Jeroboam II of Israel, roughly the early-to-mid 700s BC, but no personal birth or death year is given, so no specific date is plotted.

2 Kings 18:2 states Hezekiah was 25 when he began to reign and reigned 29 years in Jerusalem; dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology (some frameworks place his accession closer to 729 BC via a co-regency with Ahaz).

Isaiah 1:1 dates his ministry across the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (roughly the mid-700s to early 600s BC), but gives no personal birth or death year, so no specific date is plotted.
2 Kings 21:1 states Manasseh was 12 when he began to reign and reigned 55 years in Jerusalem, the longest of any king of Judah or Israel; dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology.
No birth or death year is given for Hilkiah; his high-priesthood falls under Josiah's reign, roughly the late 600s BC.
2 Kings 23:36 states Jehoiakim was 25 when he began to reign and reigned 11 years in Jerusalem; dates follow a widely-used regnal chronology.

2 Kings 24:18 states Zedekiah was 21 when he began to reign and reigned 11 years in Jerusalem; the end date here marks his capture and blinding at the fall of Jerusalem, not his eventual death in Babylonian captivity, which Scripture does not record.

Zechariah 1:1 dates the start of his ministry to two months after Haggai's, in the same second year of Darius I (520 BC), but his own birth or death year is not recorded, so no specific date is plotted.

Jeremiah 1:2-3 dates his ministry from Josiah's 13th year to Jerusalem's fall (c. 627-586 BC), an unusually well-fixed ministry span, but no personal birth or death year is given, so no specific date is plotted.

Haggai's four oracles are each dated to a specific month and day in the second year of Darius I of Persia — August through December 520 BC — an unusually precise ministry window, though his own birth or death year is not recorded, so no specific date is plotted.

Ezra 7:8 dates his return to Jerusalem to the seventh year of King Artaxerxes of Persia, but scholars genuinely dispute which Artaxerxes is meant (Artaxerxes I, c. 458 BC, or Artaxerxes II, c. 398 BC), so no specific date is plotted.
Micah 1:1 dates his ministry across the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, roughly the mid-to-late 700s BC, but gives no personal birth or death year, so no specific date is plotted.

name: King of the sons of Ammon

timeline.note: Ezekiel 1:1-2 dates his call to the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's exile (c. 593 BC), and his final dated oracle to c. 571 BC, but no personal birth or death year is given, so no specific date is plotted.
Daniel's story spans from Nebuchadnezzar's first deportation (c. 605 BC) into the reign of Cyrus of Persia (c. 530s BC), but no personal birth or death year is given, so no specific date is plotted.

name: daughter of the King of the South

timeline.note: Hosea 1:1 dates his ministry across several kings of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, roughly the mid-700s BC, but gives no personal birth or death year, so no specific date is plotted.

Joel gives no reference to a reigning king, unusual among the prophetic books, so its date is genuinely disputed among scholars, ranging from the 9th century BC to the post-exilic period; placed here in the earlier of the commonly proposed windows.
Amos 1:1 dates his ministry to the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, roughly the mid-700s BC, but gives no personal birth or death year, so no specific date is plotted.
The book's content (judgment on Edom for its role in Jerusalem's fall) points most directly to the years following 586 BC, but almost nothing about Obadiah's own life or dates is recorded.

Nahum's reference to Thebes' earlier fall (663 BC) and his announcement of Nineveh's coming destruction (612 BC) place his ministry somewhere in that window, but no personal birth or death year is given, so no specific date is plotted.

Habakkuk's description of the Babylonians (Chaldeans) as a rising power points to the late 600s BC, shortly before Judah's fall, but no personal birth or death year is given, so no specific date is plotted.
Zephaniah 1:1 dates his ministry to the reign of Josiah, likely its earlier years before the 622 BC reforms, but gives no personal birth or death year, so no specific date is plotted.

Malachi addresses a functioning, already-rebuilt temple and weary post-exilic routine, placing him after Haggai and Zechariah, likely the 5th century BC, but no specific date or personal birth/death year is recorded.
